summary: Full-extraction pass over 20 stored US documents: the SEC whistleblower annual reports FY2011-FY2019, the SEC OIG audit No. 575 (2022) and Madoff report (2009), NHTSA's 2023 NPRM and 2025 enforcement-discretion notice, the New York MFCU FCA letters and NY FCA text, FERA 2009, the 1986 FCA amendments, the FY2021 NDAA (HTML copy), and the Digital Realty and Polansky Supreme Court opinions. Most new rows come from the SEC annual reports: tips by US state for every year (region=US-XX, as extract-whistleblowing-usa9 uses), monthly tips by category for FY2011-12 (FY2012 from an image table by OCR, reconciled to row and column totals), comparison bars repeated in later reports, every Investor Protection Fund table line (all tables check to the printed closing balances), hotline calls, NoCAs, source-country counts, matters tracked, staff, award-recipient profile counts and shares, protection-enforcement counts, and Rule 21F-17/retaliation events. Conventions follow usa9 where it overlaps (fund sequestration and accrual lines, inspector_general item, protection_enforcement_actions, max_award_presumption_rate, sanctions_ordered item=returned_to_investors). One new indicator proposed (recoveries_state_incentive, NY Medicaid FCA bonus share). Quotes from OCR'd image pages (FY2012 Appendix A and B, FY2016 Appendix B, OIG 575 management response) will not match the text layer and need the second reading.

events.title: FERA amends the False Claims Act (Pub. L. 111-21, sec. 4)
events.description: The Fraud Enforcement and Recovery Act rewrites FCA liability (claims to contractors and grantees covered, "material" and "obligation" defined, reverse false claims), lets the government file its own complaint relating back to the relator's, lets the Attorney General delegate civil investigative demands and share their results with qui tam relators, extends anti-retaliation relief to contractors and agents (reinstatement, two times back pay), and allows service of sealed complaints on state co-plaintiffs. Effective on enactment; the false-record provision applies to claims pending on or after 7 June 2008.
events.quote: Any information obtained by the Attorney General or a designee of the Attorney General under this section may be shared with any qui tam relator if the Attorney General or designee determine it is necessary as part of any false claims act investigation.

events.title: SEC establishes the Office of the Whistleblower
events.description: The SEC set up OWB as a separate office within the Division of Enforcement to administer section 21F.
events.quote: On May 25, 2011, the SEC established OWB as a separate office within the SEC’s Division of Enforcement

events.title: 2020 whistleblower rule amendments take effect
events.description: Amendments adopted 23 Sep 2020 take effect, including the presumption of a maximum 30% award for awards of $5 million or less.
events.quote: On September 23, 2020, the SEC adopted amendments to Rule 21F, which became effective on December 7, 2020.

events.title: 2022 whistleblower rule amendments take effect
events.description: Amendments adopted 26 Aug 2022 take effect: broader payment for related non-SEC actions and authority to consider the dollar amount only to increase an award.
events.quote: On August 26, 2022, the SEC adopted two additional amendments to Rule 21F, which became effective on October 3, 2022.

events.title: OWB launches a modernized claims tracking system
events.description: OWB replaced its Claims Tracker spreadsheet system with a modernized system to track claims from application to payment; funding had been refused from May 2017 to June 2019.
events.quote: Then, in January 2022, OWB implemented a new system to modernize, standardize, and automate the tracking and management of whistleblower program information

events.title: Jane Norberg named OWB Deputy Chief
events.description: The Commission named Jane A. Norberg Deputy Chief of the Office of the Whistleblower.
events.quote: On January 17, 2012, the Commission named Jane A. Norberg as the Office’s Deputy Chief.

events.title: Fifth Circuit in Asadi v. G.E. Energy limits Dodd-Frank retaliation protection
events.description: The Fifth Circuit held that the Dodd-Frank anti-retaliation provision gives a private cause of action only to employees who report directly to the SEC, contrary to the SEC's rule and several district courts.
events.quote: On July 17, 2013, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in Asadi v. G.E. Energy (USA), L.L.C., 720 F 3d 620 (5th Cir 2013) held that the anti-retaliation provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act provide a private cause of action only for those employees who provide allegations of possible securities law violations directly to the Commission

events.title: SEC brings its first anti-retaliation case (Paradigm Capital Management)
events.description: The SEC charged hedge fund adviser Paradigm Capital Management and its owner with retaliating against the head trader who reported prohibited principal transactions; they agreed to pay $2.2 million to settle the retaliation and other charges.
events.quote: On June 16, 2014, the SEC exercised its anti-retaliation authority for the first time

events.title: Supreme Court: Sarbanes-Oxley protection covers employees of contractors (Lawson v. FMR)
events.description: The Supreme Court held that Sarbanes-Oxley anti-retaliation protection extends to employees of contractors of public companies; the SEC notes this also widens Dodd-Frank protection.
events.quote: the Supreme Court, on March 4, 2014, held that the Sarbanes-Oxley’s anti-retaliation protections are not limited to employees of publicly-traded companies

events.title: First SEC action under Rule 21F-17(a) against restrictive confidentiality agreements (KBR Inc.)
events.description: The SEC found that KBR's confidentiality statements for internal-investigation interviews impeded whistleblowing; KBR paid a $130,000 penalty and amended its statements.
events.quote: On April 1, 2015, the Commission brought its first enforcement action against a company for its use of confidentiality agreements that impeded whistleblowers in violation of Rule 21F-17(a) .

events.title: SEC interpretive guidance: Dodd-Frank retaliation protection covers internal reporting
events.description: The SEC released interpretive guidance that the anti-retaliation provisions protect people who report internally, even before reporting to the SEC (80 Fed. Reg. 47,829, 10 Aug 2015).
events.quote: On August 4, 2015, the Commission released interpretive guidance clarifying the interaction of the anti-retaliation provisions and the award provisions

events.title: Second Circuit in Berman v. Neo@Ogilvy defers to SEC rule on internal reporters
events.description: The Second Circuit held that Dodd-Frank retaliation protection covers employees who report to their employers, creating a circuit split with Asadi (Fifth Circuit).
events.quote: the Second Circuit in Berman v. Neo@Ogilvy LLC, held that the pertinent provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act were sufficiently ambiguous to warrant the court’s deference to the SEC’s rule

events.title: Jane Norberg becomes Chief of the Office of the Whistleblower
events.description: Jane Norberg, OWB's first Deputy Chief, was named Chief after Sean McKessy left the Commission in July 2016.
events.quote: Jane Norberg, the Office’s first Deputy Chief, was named Chief of OWB in September 2016.

events.title: Merrill Lynch charged under Rule 21F-17(a) for restrictive severance language
events.description: In its settlement over the customer protection rule ($415 million), Merrill Lynch was also charged with using severance-agreement language that impeded employees from reporting to the SEC.
events.quote: On June 23, 2016, in connection with the SEC’s administrative settlement with Merrill Lynch for violations of the customer protection rule, the Commission also charged Merrill Lynch with violating Rule 21F-17(a)

events.title: BlueLinx pays $265,000 for severance agreements waiving SEC award rights
events.description: First stand-alone Rule 21F-17(a) case in FY2016: BlueLinx Holdings required departing employees to waive monetary recovery from complaints to the SEC.
events.quote: BlueLinx agreed to pay a $265,000 civil penalty

events.title: Health Net pays $340,000 for severance agreements waiving SEC whistleblower awards
events.description: Health Net required departing employees to waive SEC whistleblower awards as a condition of severance (Rule 21F-17(a)).
events.quote: Health Net agreed to pay a $340,000 civil penalty

events.title: AB InBev charged under Rule 21F-17(a) over a separation agreement
events.description: A separation agreement with liquidated damages stopped an employee from continuing to talk to the SEC; also FCPA books-and-records charges.
events.quote: on September 28, 2016, the Commission instituted proceedings against Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV (ABI InBev) for violations of Rule 21F-17(a)

events.title: First stand-alone SEC whistleblower retaliation case (International Game Technology)
events.description: IGT fired a director who reported possible accounting distortions to management and the SEC; it paid a $500,000 civil penalty.
events.quote: On September 29, 2016, the Commission brought its first stand-alone retaliation case under Section 21F(h)(1) of the Exchange Act.

events.title: NeuStar pays $180,000 for severance agreements barring talk with the SEC (Rule 21F-17)
events.description: NeuStar's non-disparagement clauses, signed by at least 246 departing employees, named the SEC and risked forfeiting all but $100 of severance.
events.quote: NeuStar also agreed to pay a civil money penalty of $180,000 to the Commission.

events.title: SandRidge Energy pays $1.4 million for retaliation and restrictive separation agreements
events.description: SandRidge fired an employee who raised internal concerns about reserves calculations and used separation agreements barring cooperation with government investigations (over 500 signatories).
events.quote: SandRidge agreed to pay a penalty of $1.4 million.

events.title: BlackRock pays $340,000 for separation agreements waiving whistleblower awards
events.description: Over 1,000 departing employees signed agreements waiving recovery of incentives for reporting misconduct, including under Dodd-Frank.
events.quote: BlackRock agreed to pay a $340,000 penalty to settle the charges.

events.title: HomeStreet pays $500,000 after trying to identify a whistleblower (Rule 21F-17)
events.description: HomeStreet sought to unmask a presumed whistleblower, suggested denying legal-cost indemnification, and used severance agreements waiving awards.
events.quote: HomeStreet additionally agreed to pay a civil money penalty of $500,000 to the Commission.

events.title: Emily Pasquinelli becomes OWB Deputy Chief
events.description: Promoted to Deputy Chief, filling the post vacated when Jane Norberg became Chief.
events.quote: In May 2017, Emily Pasquinelli was promoted to Deputy Chief

events.title: Supreme Court grants certiorari in Digital Realty Trust v. Somers
events.description: The Court agreed to decide whether Dodd-Frank retaliation protection covers employees who report only internally; the Solicitor General, joined by the SEC, filed a brief for the whistleblower on 17 Oct 2017.
events.quote: On June 26, 2017, on the basis of the circuit split, the United States Supreme Court granted certiorari in Digital Realty Trust, Inc. v. Somers

events.title: Second Circuit upholds SEC denial of late award claims (Cerny v. SEC)
events.description: The court affirmed the denial of two claimants whose applications were filed about two years after the 90-day deadline.
events.quote: The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit recently upheld the Commission’s denial of two claimants whose award applications were submitted approximately two years after the required deadline.

events.title: SEC v. Crumbley and Sedona Oil & Gas settled: injunction under Rule 21F-17
events.description: The defendant, who threatened to fire employees for talking to the SEC, was enjoined from future Rule 21F-17 violations as part of a settlement at the end of FY2018.
events.quote: settled at the end of FY 2018

new_indicators.name: State bonus share of Medicaid fraud recoveries
new_indicators.definition: Money from Medicaid false-claims recoveries that a US state keeps instead of returning it to the federal government because its own false claims act qualifies under section 1909 of the Social Security Act (an extra 10 percentage points of the federal share), in a period, as printed by the source.
new_indicators.notes: proposed by extract-whistleblowing-usa8 (New York MFCU annual letters 2018-2020).

ledger.contains: Notice of proposed rulemaking for NHTSA's motor vehicle safety whistleblower program (49 CFR Part 513), 88 FR 23276, 14 Apr 2023, 47 pp.: background (FAST Act 2015, more than 150 whistleblower submissions since 2015, the Hyundai/Kia award), comparison with SEC, CFTC, IRS and FCA programmes, section-by-section discussion of proposed definitions, submission, confidentiality, eligibility, 90-day claim deadline, award determination (10-30%), appeals and payment, regulatory analyses with Paperwork Reduction Act estimates (50 WB-INFO, 45 WB-RELEASE, 2 WB-AWARD forms a year, 1-2 Notices of Covered Action a year, burden hours and lawyer costs), the proposed regulatory text and forms WB-INFO, WB-RELEASE, WB-AWARD. Also relays SEC figures (tips from about 130 countries; 99 foreign countries in FY2021; 19 foreign award recipients). Added the PRA projections, the SEC relayed figures, the statutory rules restated, and the Hyundai/Kia case as this source describes it. Not recorded: proposed (not adopted) rules such as the 90-day claim deadline, anonymous filing through a lawyer and 30-day appeal window, which the final rule (usa-nhtsa-wb-finalrule-2024) already gives as adopted rules; PRA burden hours and lawyer cost estimates (paperwork cost, no indicator); the "more than 150 submissions" repeated on p. 27 (same claim as the existing p. 2 row); the $100 million example and $3,000,000 instalment example (illustrations); CBP's 7.8 million imported items (not about the programme). The SEC count of 14 Rule 21F-17 actions (footnote 50) is recorded under the proposed indicator protection_enforcement_actions.

Federal Register pages 90 FR 11029-11030 (3 Mar 2025, 2 pp.). Contains NHTSA's notification of enforcement discretion: the whistleblower final rule (89 FR 101952, 17 Dec 2024) took effect on 16 Jan 2025, and NHTSA will not enforce it until 20 Mar 2025 so that the new administration's officials can review it. The same pages also carry two unrelated documents: an HHS policy statement rescinding the Richardson Waiver, and a NHTSA enforcement-discretion notice for the bus rollover safety standard. No numbers about the programme. The 3 Mar 2025 event is already recorded; the 16 Jan 2025 effective date is already covered by the final-rule event and rules (usa-nhtsa-wb-finalrule-2024). Nothing new added.

Three annual letters (15 Apr 2019, 11 May 2020, 15 Apr 2021; 3 pp., obtained under FOIL) from the New York AG's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit to the legislature under State Finance Law 190-b: MFCU recoveries under the New York False Claims Act for calendar years 2018, 2019 and 2020, and for each year the amount kept by the state Medicaid programme rather than sent to the federal government because the state act qualifies under section 1909 of the Social Security Act (60% instead of 50% share). The three recovery totals were already recorded; added the three state-incentive amounts under a proposed indicator. The letters do not split recoveries by qui tam or not, and give no relator shares. Note: the PDF page order is 2018, 2019, 2020 letters while the FOIL Bates numbers run 000001, 000003, 000002; the existing rows cite the Bates number as the page.

Text of the New York False Claims Act, State Finance Law Art. 13, §§ 187-194, with amendments through 2018 (10 pp.): definitions, liability (civil penalty of $6,000-$12,000 per claim, adjusted to the federal level, plus treble damages; double damages for self-reporting within 30 days), the tax-law conditions (defendant net income or sales of at least $1 million and damages pleaded over $350,000), civil enforcement and qui tam actions (complaint under seal for at least 60 days, state may supersede or intervene within 60 days), parties' rights, relator awards (15-25% if the state intervenes or converts, 25-30% if not, at most 10% if based mainly on public disclosures; reduction for planners, none if convicted), public-disclosure bar, the annual MFCU recovery report (§ 190-b, due 15 April), anti-retaliation remedies (two times back pay), 10-year limitation period. No statistics. The five relator-share rules were already recorded; added the two tax-law thresholds. Not recorded because the data model has no rule type for them: penalty per claim, seal period, intervention window, limitation period, retaliation remedies.

Public Law 111-21, Fraud Enforcement and Recovery Act of 2009 (FERA), 20 May 2009, 15 pp.: sec. 2 widens federal fraud crimes (mortgage lending businesses, TARP and stimulus funds, commodities fraud, money-laundering proceeds); sec. 3 authorises extra appropriations against fraud for FY2010-2011 ($165 million a year for DOJ, of which $15 million for the Civil Division; $30 million each for the Postal Inspection Service and HUD OIG; $20 million each for the Secret Service and SEC enforcement; $1 million for SEC OIG) — general enforcement budgets, not money for whistleblower rewards, so not recorded; sec. 4 amends the False Claims Act (liability rewritten, civil penalty $5,000-$10,000 plus treble damages, government complaints relate back to the relator's, civil investigative demands may be delegated and shared with qui tam relators, anti-retaliation relief for employees, contractors and agents including two times back pay, seal does not prevent serving state co-plaintiffs; effective dates incl. retroactivity to 7 June 2008); sec. 5 creates the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission (out of scope). No change to relator award percentages, so no rule rows. Added one event for sec. 4 from this source (an event for FERA existed only from the CRS report).

HTML copy of Public Law 116-283, the NDAA for FY2021 (whole law, 5.5 MB). The same law is also stored as the signed PDF (usa-congress-pl116-283-2021, a different file), which an earlier pass reviewed as complete. Searched the whole text for whistleblower, reward, informant and qui tam provisions: in scope are sec. 6314 (AML Act of 2020, rewrites 31 U.S.C. 5323: FinCEN/BSA whistleblower awards up to 30% of collected sanctions over $1,000,000, discretion, exclusions, anonymous claims through counsel, 30-day appeal, anti-retaliation, confidentiality; 134 Stat. 4597-4603) and sec. 9701-9703 (Kleptocracy Asset Recovery Rewards pilot; 134 Stat. 4834-4837). Everything in those sections is already recorded: the three kleptocracy rules and the enactment event from this HTML copy, the AML rules, the perjury rule and the $450,000 FY2021 authorisation from the PDF copy. Nothing added here, to avoid double rows. Out of scope: sec. 1238 (State Department rewards for information on foreign election interference, not a programme in this dataset), federal-employee and Coast Guard whistleblower protections, DoD skills rewards, and the rest of the defence law.

Public Law 99-562, False Claims Amendments Act of 1986, 27 Oct 1986 (100 Stat. 3153-3169, 17 pp., scanned text layer): sec. 2 rewrites FCA liability (penalty $5,000-$10,000 plus treble damages; double damages for self-reporting within 30 days; "knowing" and "claim" defined); sec. 3 rewrites 31 U.S.C. 3730 (qui tam suits filed under seal for at least 60 days, 60 days for the government to intervene, parties' rights, relator share 15-25% if the government proceeds, at most 10% if based mainly on public disclosures, 25-30% if it does not, public-disclosure bar with original-source exception, bars on suits against members of the armed forces, Congress, judiciary and senior officials); sec. 4 anti-retaliation relief (two times back pay); sec. 5 limitation periods (6 years, or 3 years after discovery, max 10); sec. 6 jurisdiction and civil investigative demands (31 U.S.C. 3732-3733, procedure); sec. 7 criminal penalties; legislative history. No statistics. The five relator-share rules, the public-disclosure bar and the enactment event were already recorded from this document; nothing new to add (penalty amounts, seal and intervention periods, limitation periods and retaliation remedies have no rule type in the data model).

US Supreme Court slip opinion, Digital Realty Trust, Inc. v. Somers, No. 16-1276, decided 21 Feb 2018 (29 pp.: syllabus, opinion of the Court by Justice Ginsburg, concurrences by Justices Sotomayor and Thomas). Holds that Dodd-Frank's anti-retaliation provision protects only people who reported to the SEC; compares Sarbanes-Oxley (180-day complaint deadline, actual back pay) with Dodd-Frank (direct suit, six-year limit, double back pay); describes the SEC award (10-30% of collected sanctions) and Rule 21F-2; Paul Somers (named by the Court) was a Digital Realty vice president 2010-2014 who reported internally only. One statistic: about 80% of 2016 award recipients reported internally first (Solicitor General, relayed). The event was already recorded; added the relayed 80% share and the award range as the Court states it. No case row: Somers is a retaliation suit, not an award or reward case.

US Supreme Court slip opinion, United States ex rel. Polansky v. Executive Health Resources, Inc., No. 21-1052, decided 16 Jun 2023 (37 pp.: syllabus, opinion of the Court by Justice Kagan, concurrence by Justice Kavanaugh, dissent by Justice Thomas, appendix with 31 U.S.C. 3730 text). Holds that the government may move to dismiss a qui tam suit whenever it has intervened, and that Rule 41(a) governs such motions. Describes the FCA scheme (relator share up to 30%; 60-day seal; later intervention for good cause), the facts of Polansky's 2012 qui tam suit, and (dissent) the 15-25% and 25-30% ranges. No statistics. The event was already recorded; added the relator-share rules as the Court and the dissent state them, and the Polansky suit as a case (dismissed, no recovery).

SEC Office of Inspector General audit report No. 575, 19 Dec 2022 (43 pp.; management comments pp. 39-42 are images, read by OCR): SEC whistleblower programme growth and controls, FY2017-FY2021. Contains: cumulative figures (sanctions ordered $6.3 billion, more than $1.5 billion returned to investors, more than $1.3 billion awarded to over 300 individuals); Table 1 (tips, claims, individuals awarded and amount awarded per FY 2017-2021 with totals); Figure 2 (tips FY2011-2021); Figure 3 (days from NoCA close to draft declaration and total processing time, before/after May 2019); Figure 4 (claims received vs processed FY2017-2021); backlog (299 old claims processed FY2020-21, 151 still open Sept 2022); OWB staff (about 16 in FY2017, at least 25 in FY2021); rules (threshold, 10-30%, $5m max-award presumption, 90-day claim deadline, 30/60/30-day steps, $300m fund replenishment); rule-amendment dates; hotline (15,087 voicemails FY2017-21; over 30,000 calls returned since 2011); 98 Final Orders in FY2021; one award of about $500,000; audit-sample control findings and eight recommendations. Tables checked: Table 1 columns and Figure 4 add to their totals; 230+299 = FY2020+FY2021 processed. Also added: 89% use of the max-award presumption (relayed, indicator proposed by usa9). Not recorded: shares of the 29-package audit sample (51% of time on declarations, 13% approved with most CRS members absent, 96% adopted unchanged, 41% delayed 122-852 days), 47 outreach engagements, 438 claims packages in scope, hotline timeliness splits beyond the note, 14 late Final Order postings, the $159,000 data-entry error.
ledger.to_do: Two programme numbers have no indicator and are not recorded: 47 outreach engagements FY2017-FY2021 (PDF pp. 26-27); 438 claims packages with at least one claimant FY2017-FY2021 (PDF pp. 12, 34). Record them if indicators for outreach events and NoCAs with claimants are added. Audit-sample control-test shares (51%, 13%, 96%, 41%) and the $159,000 data error are audit findings, deliberately not recorded.

ledger.contains: SEC Office of Inspector General, Investigation of Failure of the SEC to Uncover Bernard Madoff's Ponzi Scheme, public version, Report No. OIG-509, 31 Aug 2009 (477 pp.): how the SEC handled six substantive complaints about Madoff from 1992 to 2008 (including Harry Markopolos's 2000, 2001 and 2005 submissions), its examinations and investigations, and why they failed. It predates the Dodd-Frank reward programme; the only reward-related content is the Enforcement staff's suspicion that Markopolos "was looking for a bounty" and the report's note that he would not have been eligible for the insider-trading bounty (Exchange Act s. 21A(e)) in a Ponzi case (PDF pp. ~23, 248-249, and the conclusions). No programme statistics, rules or awards. Method: the 477-page report was searched in full text for bounty, reward, whistleblower and informant passages and those passages read; the rest is investigative narrative about Madoff, out of scope. The scandal event and the Markopolos case were already recorded; nothing new added.
